title: Verifier-Guided Prompting for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered NetOps Study
abstract: We study whether constrained prompting combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback (generate→verify→repair) increases the semantic correctness of translating operator natural-language intents into low-level network configuration sequences. We preregistered a paired confirmatory experiment (N=150 synthetic intents, four intent families; paired baseline vs guarded, shared_initial_candidate semantics) using a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) and a deterministic network validator. Primary outcome was verifier pass/fail per condition. Results: baseline success = 149/150 (99.33%), guarded success = 150/150 (100%), paired absolute difference = 0.67 percentage points, exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap CI for the difference = [0.00, 0.02]. Exploratory diagnostics show a single guarded repair call occurred (1/150). Interpretation: in this synthetic task corpus the guarded workflow did not produce a statistically or practically meaningful improvement over an already high-performing baseline; the experiment instead exposes a ceiling effect and highlights design fragility when baseline correctness is high. We report the preregistration, full execution manifest, analyses, and limitations; we bound claims to the synthetic corpus, single model, and verifier harness used.

sections.introduction: Modern network operations increasingly explore natural-language intent interfaces and LLM-assisted automation, but operational adoption depends on reliably translating high-level intent into safe, correct low-level configuration sequences. Prior work shows LLMs can generate useful configuration templates yet often produce syntactic or semantic errors that require downstream correction [1], and a growing body of work advocates integrate-then-verify pipelines that combine generation with deterministic verifiers and iterative repair to improve correctness in infrastructure-as-code and configuration tasks [2], [3]. At the same time, agentic LLM pipelines that enact tool calls are vulnerable to prompt-injection and claim-to-action failures unless guarded by verifier-aware controls [4]. Operationally meaningful evaluation therefore requires end-to-end measurement linking generated changes to deterministic network-level validation oracles [3], [5]. Our study asks: Does combining constrained prompting (structured templates + explicit semantic slots) with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback materially increase semantic-correctness when translating operator intents into configurations, compared to an unconstrained baseline prompt? We preregistered a paired experiment and executed it end-to-end with archived artifacts; this paper reports the confirmatory and exploratory findings, diagnostics, and threats to validity.
sections.related_work: Several strands of literature inform our design. Intent-to-configuration translation and LLM-driven intent translation have been explored with fine-tuning and in-context learning, but reviews report modest NL→formal-spec semantic-correctness and emphasize remaining gaps in reliably producing verifier-sound specifications [1]. Neuro-symbolic and verifier-guided approaches in IaC and configuration generation (e.g., TerraFormer) show that verifier feedback during training or inference can reduce errors and policy violations in infrastructure artifacts [2]. Benchmarks that couple generation with formal verification (e.g., Cornetto) have begun to quantify LLM performance on configuration repair at scale and demonstrate that even state-of-the-art models often introduce regressions absent verifier integration [3]. Security analyses of tool-using agents document how false textual claims can be transformed into harmful actions in multi-tool pipelines, motivating gatekeeping and deterministic validation as defensive primitives [4]. Finally, a mature ecosystem of network verification tools (NetKAT/KATch, ShapeShifter/ACORN, Hoyan, etc.) provides deterministic reachability and policy checks that can act as authoritative validators in controlled experiments [5]. Our work builds on these findings by preregistering and executing a tightly specified generate→verify→repair confirmatory trial that measures verifier-level correctness as the primary outcome.
sections.methodology: Preregistered design: Study ID study_cand_2026_b2_v1 (frozen preregistration) specified a paired confirmatory comparison of two conditions: (A) baseline free-text prompt and (C) constrained template prompt plus deterministic verifier-guided single-repair attempt (guarded). The study used shared_initial_candidate semantics (the same initial generation served as the starting candidate for both conditions), per the preregistration semantics. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (verifier pass/fail). Planned N=150 confirmatory intents (50 per intent family), paired episodes = 300. Model: gpt-5-mini (hosted via openai_responses adapter). Verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (used as the binary oracle that assesses whether the produced configuration satisfies the preregistered formal intent constraints and preserved-state policies). Task generation: deterministic synthetic corpus restricted to four intent families (reachability/isolation/ACL/QoS-like workflow constraints) and topologies sized for the verifier (toy-to-small, 4–32 nodes) as specified in the preregistration. Execution contract limited each episode to one initial model call and at most one additional guarded repair call; total model calls used = 151. Analysis plan: primary confirmatory paired binary test implemented via exact McNemar two-sided test with 10,000 bootstrap resamples for 95% CIs; predefined multiplicity correction for two secondary contrasts. Inclusion/exclusion: rule-based ambiguity detector excluded ambiguous intents pre-call (none were excluded during the run). All mapping code, verifier inputs, raw model outputs, and logs were archived per the execution manifest.
sections.results: Execution and primary outcome: All planned confirmatory intents completed (complete_pair_count = 150; completed_episode_count = 300). Contingency counts: both-pass (n_11) = 149, baseline-only-pass (n_01)=0, guarded-only-pass (n_10)=1, both-fail (n_00)=0. Per-condition success rates: baseline = 149/150 = 0.9933, guarded = 150/150 = 1.0. Estimated paired absolute difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00667 (0.67 percentage points). Statistical test: exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% paired-bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Exploratory diagnostics: only one repair-stage invocation occurred (repair stage count = 1), implying the constrained+verifier pipeline requested repair in a single case; median revision iterations in guarded episodes = 0 (IQR=0). Missingness/exclusions: none. Contamination checks: none observed. The confirmatory preregistered contrast therefore fails to provide evidence of a meaningful improvement by the guarded workflow on this synthetic corpus: the baseline was already near-ceiling and the observed absolute improvement is both numerically tiny and statistically non-significant under the preregistered test.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: The guarded generate→verify→repair workflow did not materially improve verifier-level semantic correctness in this preregistered synthetic corpus because the unconstrained baseline achieved near-perfect correctness. This outcome reflects a ceiling effect rather than evidence that verifier-guided repair is universally unnecessary. Practical implications: (i) In tasks or corpora where base-model correctness is already near 100%, single-repair guarded pipelines may produce marginal returns; (ii) Guarded pipelines still serve defensive roles (auditability, explicit validation) even when they do not change pass rates; (iii) experimental design must anticipate baseline competence to avoid underpowered or mismatched confirmatory plans. Relation to prior work: our findings are consistent with prior reports that verifier-guided methods can improve correctness on harder benchmarks and larger-scale settings [2], [3], but also underscore Cornetto-like observations that gains shrink when tasks are simpler or models are highly capable on the chosen corpus [3]. The single-model, synthetic-corpus result does not contradict evidence that verifier guidance and iterative repair are valuable in broader, more diverse, or higher-complexity scenarios. Failure-mode analysis: the dominant residual failure mode in our setup is design fragility—preregistration assumed a baseline ≈35% and powered for a 15pp absolute increase; the actual baseline (≈99%) invalidated those power assumptions and demonstrates the importance of pilot calibration. Operational implications: practitioners seeking to deploy LLM-assisted NetOps should (a) baseline-measure model competence on representative production tasks before choosing guarded vs lightweight workflows, (b) provision deterministic validators as mandatory safety gates, and (c) instrument repair-loop utilization to track when LLMs actually benefit from verifier feedback.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, paired confirmatory trial that measured verifier-level semantic correctness for intent-to-configuration translation using gpt-5-mini on a deterministically generated synthetic intent corpus. The constrained prompting plus deterministic verifier-guided single-repair workflow produced no material improvement over an already high-performing baseline (149/150 → 150/150). The principal scientific lesson is methodological: preregistered confirmatory trials in LLM-for-NetOps require careful pilot calibration of baseline competence to avoid ceiling effects and mismatched power assumptions. Technically, our results do not imply that verifier-guided repair is unnecessary; rather, they demonstrate that gains are context- and corpus-dependent. We publish the preregistration, execution manifest, raw model outputs, verifier verdicts, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducible reanalysis and to inform future studies that target production-scale heterogeneity and adversarial or low-baseline regimes where verifier-guided repair is more likely to yield substantive improvements.

limitations: Single-model constraint: experiments used only gpt-5-mini; results do not generalize across models or sizes.

Synthetic corpus and scale: tasks were programmatically generated and limited to verifier-capable toy-to-small topologies (4–32 nodes); external validity to production WANs and heterogeneous vendor CLIs is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract limited repair budget to a single guarded repair call per intent; different generation semantics or multiple-repair budgets may yield different outcomes.

Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch: baseline correctness was far higher than pilot assumptions used for power calculations (planned effect size 15pp), reducing the trial's ability to demonstrate benefit and illustrating sensitivity to baseline calibration.

Verifier coverage and specification translation: the study measures verifier pass/fail on the preregistered invariants but does not claim full operational safety guarantees beyond the deterministic validator's modeled properties.

Security and adversarial robustness: the experiment did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection or adversary-driven intents; separate targeted studies are needed to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities in agentic NetOps workflows.
